---
title: "Cooperativity: the Hill model"
description: "Fit the Hill model to sigmoidal rate data, compare it with Michaelis-Menten, and read the Hill coefficient."
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.2, out.width = "100%")
```

Some enzymes respond to substrate cooperatively: binding at one site makes binding at others easier, and the rate curve is sigmoidal rather than hyperbolic. The Hill model (`"HILL"`) describes curves like this empirically. This example simulates cooperative data, fits both the Hill and Michaelis-Menten (`"MM"`) models, and shows how the residuals tell them apart.

```{r}
library(enzKinet2)
```

## The Hill model

```{r}
print(MODEL_FORMULAE[["HILL"]], showEnv = FALSE)
```

The Hill model has three parameters:

- `Vmax`, the limiting rate.
- `n`, the Hill coefficient. With n = 1 the Hill model is the Michaelis-Menten equation. n greater than 1 means positive cooperativity (a sigmoidal curve), and n less than 1 negative cooperativity.
- `Km`, the substrate concentration that gives half of Vmax. In the Hill model this is the half-saturation constant, K0.5. It is named `Km` in enzKinet2, but it isn't a Michaelis constant, because the Hill equation isn't the Michaelis-Menten equation unless n = 1.

## Simulate cooperative data

```{r}
set.seed(11)
data <- simulate_data("HILL", list(Km = 1, Vmax = 10, n = 2.5), x.min = 0.1, x.max = 4,
                      n.samples = 12, n.replicates = 2, noise.level = 0.05)
make_plot("HILL", data.df = data, x.units = "mM", y.units = "µM/min")
```

The rise is slow at low concentrations, then steep around 1 mM: the sigmoidal shape of cooperativity.

## Fit both models

```{r}
fit_hill <- fit_model("HILL", data, start.params = list(Km = 1, Vmax = 8, n = 1),
                      get.conf.int = TRUE, get.stats = TRUE)
fit_mm <- fit_model("MM", data, start.params = list(Km = 1, Vmax = 8), get.stats = TRUE)
round(unlist(fit_hill$fitted.params), 3)
round(unlist(fit_mm$fitted.params), 3)
c(HILL = fit_hill$statistics$AIC, MM = fit_mm$statistics$AIC)
```

Starting the Hill fit at n = 1, the Michaelis-Menten case, works here: the fit moves n to about `r round(fit_hill$fitted.params$n, 1)`, and its confidence interval excludes 1, which is evidence of cooperativity. The Hill model's AIC is far lower. The Michaelis-Menten fit makes up for the wrong shape with a larger Km and Vmax.

## Compare the fits and residuals

```{r}
curve_hill <- make_curve("HILL", fit_hill$fitted.params, x.min = 0, x.max = 4)
curve_mm <- make_curve("MM", fit_mm$fitted.params, x.min = 0, x.max = 4)
make_plot("HILL", data.df = data, curve.df = curve_hill, extra.curve = curve_mm,
          x.units = "mM", y.units = "µM/min",
          title = "Hill fit (coloured) and Michaelis-Menten fit (black)")
```

```{r}
make_residual_plot("HILL", fit_hill$fitted.params, data, x.units = "mM", y.units = "µM/min",
                   title = "Hill residuals")
make_residual_plot("MM", fit_mm$fitted.params, data, x.units = "mM", y.units = "µM/min",
                   title = "Michaelis-Menten residuals")
```

The Hill residuals scatter around zero. The Michaelis-Menten residuals follow a pattern: negative at low concentrations, positive in the middle and negative again at the top. A run of residuals with the same sign like this is the usual sign of the wrong model.

## Plots for the Hill model

The Lineweaver-Burk, Hanes and Eadie-Hofstee plots only straighten Michaelis-Menten curves, and the direct linear plot is for Michaelis-Menten only. enzKinet2 doesn't allow them for the Hill model:

```{r}
BLOCKED_TRANSFORMATIONS[["HILL"]]
```

The log10 plot (v against log10 a) is allowed, and suits a sigmoidal curve, spreading out the low concentrations:

```{r}
curve_log <- make_curve("HILL", fit_hill$fitted.params, x.min = 0.1, x.max = 4)
make_plot("HILL", data.df = data, curve.df = curve_log, plot.transformation = "log10",
          x.units = "mM", y.units = "µM/min")
```

The curve starts at 0.1 mM, because log10(0) is undefined. For binding with cooperativity, the Hill Binding Kinetics model (`"BKH"`) is the equivalent: see the [model gallery](../concepts/models.html).
